title: What is archaeology? Meaning, methods and Indian examples
seo_title: What is Archaeology? Meaning, Scope and Methods in India
meta_description: What is archaeology? A clear explanation of its meaning, scope, branches and methods, with Indian examples from Bhimbetka and Dholavira to Keeladi.
summary: Archaeology is the study of the human past through the material remains people left behind: tools, pottery, buildings, bones, seeds, coins, inscriptions and the soil layers that hold them. It covers everything from the first stone tools over a million years old to the recent past, and it works where written records are absent, silent or one-sided.

sections.h2: Archaeology meaning: studying people through things
paras: The word comes from the Greek archaios (ancient) and logos (study), but the modern discipline is less about antiquity for its own sake and more about people. An archaeologist looks at a broken pot, a hearth, a posthole or a grain of charred rice and asks what someone was doing, when, and why. The object matters because of the human behaviour it records.

That is why context is everything. A coin in a museum case tells you about the coin. The same coin found sealed under a floor, beside a hearth and a particular type of pottery, tells you roughly when that floor was laid and what people were cooking and trading at the time. Most of an archaeologist's effort goes into recording context before it is destroyed by digging.

Archaeology overlaps with history but is not the same thing. History mostly works from written sources; archaeology works from material evidence and can reach periods and people that texts ignore. Our page on the [difference between archaeology and history](difference-between-archaeology-and-history.html) sets out how the two meet.

sections.h2: What does archaeology study? The scope of the subject
paras: The scope of archaeology is the entire human past, from the earliest hominins to the twentieth century. In India this runs from Acheulian hand axes at sites such as Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu, through the painted shelters of Bhimbetka and the cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, to medieval forts, colonial cemeteries and industrial remains.

Archaeologists study artefacts (things people made or used), ecofacts (plant and animal remains, pollen, soils), features (pits, walls, hearths, drains that cannot be lifted) and sites (places where these occur together). They also study the wider setting: rivers that shifted, coastlines that moved, forests that were cleared.
Archaeology splits into specialisms by period, by method and by type of evidence. A working team on an Indian excavation will usually include several of them.
list: Prehistoric archaeology: the long period before writing, including the Stone Age; see our guide to the [Stone Age in India](stone-age-in-india.html).
Protohistoric archaeology: cultures such as the Harappans, whose script exists but cannot yet be read.
Historical archaeology: periods with written records, from the Mauryas onward in India.
Epigraphy and numismatics: the study of inscriptions and coins, both key to dating.
Environmental archaeology: archaeobotany, archaeozoology and geoarchaeology, which reconstruct diet, farming and climate.
Bioarchaeology: the study of human skeletal remains for age, health, diet and, increasingly, ancient DNA.
Underwater and maritime archaeology: shipwrecks, ports and submerged sites.
Archaeological science: dating methods, residue analysis, isotopes and materials analysis.

sections.h2: How archaeologists work: survey, excavation and analysis
paras: Fieldwork usually begins with survey. Archaeologists walk fields and riverbanks looking for pottery scatters and mounds, study old maps and satellite images, and talk to villagers who often know exactly where old bricks turn up. Many sites are recorded this way without a spade going in.

Excavation is slower and more destructive, so it is done only when there is a clear research question or a site is under threat. The team lays out trenches, removes soil layer by layer, and records every layer, feature and find with drawings, photographs and written notes. Our step-by-step guide to [how an excavation works](how-an-excavation-works.html) explains the process.

Most of the work happens after the dig. Pottery is washed and classified, bones and seeds are identified, samples go to laboratories for dating, and the results are written up. A season of a few weeks in the field can mean years of analysis. If you want to feel how slow and careful this is, a [practice excavation in a mock trench](mock-trench-a-practice-excavation.html) lets a class dig, record and interpret layers without harming a real site.

Large parts of India's past are known only through archaeology. Nobody wrote down how the first farmers lived at Mehrgarh, how Dholavira managed its water, or what people ate at Neolithic Burzahom in Kashmir. Excavation and science are the only ways in.

Archaeology also tests and adds to written history. Excavations at Keeladi in Tamil Nadu have given a material picture of urban life in the early historic Tamil country. Inscriptions and coins found in the ground have fixed the dates of kings who were otherwise known only from later texts. Where texts were written by and for elites, archaeology often shows how ordinary households lived.

sections.h2: Who carries out archaeology in India?
paras: The Archaeological Survey of India, set up in 1861, protects nationally important monuments and licenses excavations; our guide to the [Archaeological Survey of India](archaeological-survey-of-india.html) covers its work. State departments of archaeology protect sites of state importance. Universities and research institutes such as Deccan College in Pune run excavations and train students, and museums hold and study the finds.

If the subject interests you as a career, read [how to become an archaeologist in India](how-to-become-an-archaeologist-in-india.html). For a short practical introduction, our session on [what archaeologists actually do](what-archaeologists-actually-do.html) walks a group through the work with real examples.

Archaeology is not treasure hunting. Most finds are potsherds, animal bones and soil samples, and their value lies in what they say about the past, not their price. Archaeologists do not study dinosaurs either: that is palaeontology. And digging is a small part of the job; recording, analysis and publication take far longer.

Another common idea is that archaeology proves or disproves stories. In practice it produces evidence that has to be interpreted, and good archaeologists say clearly where the evidence is strong and where it is thin.

faq.q: What is archaeology in simple words?
faq.a: Archaeology is the study of how people lived in the past using the things they left behind, such as tools, pottery, buildings, bones and seeds. Archaeologists find these remains through survey and excavation, record where they lay, and analyse them to understand daily life, technology, trade and belief.

faq.q: What is the difference between archaeology and anthropology?
faq.a: Anthropology studies human societies and cultures in general, past and present. Archaeology is often treated as one branch of anthropology, especially in North America, focusing on the past through material remains. In India archaeology is usually taught alongside ancient history, while anthropology has its own departments.

faq.q: Who is called the father of Indian archaeology?
faq.a: Alexander Cunningham is usually called the father of Indian archaeology. A British army engineer, he became the first head of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1861 and spent decades surveying Buddhist and other sites across north India, identifying many places named in ancient texts.

faq.q: Is archaeology a science or a humanities subject?
faq.a: It is both. Archaeology asks historical questions about people and societies, which makes it a humanities subject, but it relies heavily on scientific methods such as radiocarbon dating, soil analysis and the study of bones and plant remains. In India it is usually taught in history or archaeology departments.

faq.q: Can I study archaeology after Class 12?
faq.a: Yes. A few universities offer archaeology at undergraduate level, but the usual route is a BA in history or a related subject followed by an MA in archaeology or ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology. Our guide to archaeology courses in India lists the main options.

posts.caption: That is palaeontology. Archaeology studies people, through the pots, bones, seeds and walls they left behind. A single charred grain can tell us what was cooked in a house 4,000 years ago.

posts.hook: Next time you see a potsherd in a museum, ask where it was found.
posts.caption: An object out of context tells you about the object. Found under a floor beside a hearth, it dates the floor and tells you about the household. Context is what archaeologists record first.
